\section[comisteis · tuvisteis]{comisteis · tuvisteis — the last gap closes}

\label{lesson:ES-C63-comisteis}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Hablasteis}. Now the other two families, and then the hard stems.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -isteis, for everything else}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{comer} & \emph{\textbf{comisteis}} \\
\emph{vivir} & \emph{\textbf{vivisteis}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One ending for both, exactly as everywhere else in the preterite. The \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} families stopped being two families the first time you met this tense.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and the strong stems take it too}]
The stems that gave you trouble — \emph{tuv-}, \emph{hic-}, \emph{estuv-}, \emph{dij-} — take the same \emph{-isteis}, with no surprises left in them:

\emph{tuvisteis · hicisteis · estuvisteis · dijisteis}

And \emph{ser}/\emph{ir}, which share one past: \emph{\textbf{fuisteis}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
That was the last hole. \textbf{The preterite is finished} — every family, every person, regular and strong alike, with nothing outstanding.

It has taken a long stretch of this book to build, and it is the largest single structure in it. The review that named this debt out loud can now be read without a caveat.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{comisteis}, \emph{vivisteis}, \emph{tuvisteis}
  \item \emph{fuisteis}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending do the strong stems take? (The \textbf{same} \emph{-isteis}.)

And what is still missing from the preterite? (\textbf{Nothing.})
\end{tcolorbox}
